title: 22. Interview: Time Series Databases
summary: Interview Q&A for Time Series Databases — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Time Series Databases interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why are time series databases 10–100× faster than general-purpose databases for time-series workloads?
**Answer:** Three structural advantages compound. **(1) Storage engine matches the workload**: TSDBs use LSM-trees or append-only columnar files because writes are append-only (never update old points). General-purpose DBs use B-trees optimized for random access and updates — wasteful for time series. The write path in a TSDB is sequential append + in-memory MemTable, ~1M points/sec/node, vs. ~10k inserts/sec for PostgreSQL on the same hardware. **(2) Compression exploits time-series structure**: timestamps are delta-of-delta encoded (regular sampling → ~1 bit per timestamp vs. 64 bits); floats are Gorilla-XOR encoded (slow-changing values → 10× compression); strings are dictionary-encoded. Combined, 10–100× compression means more data fits in RAM/cache, dramatically speeding up scans. **(3) Query patterns match storage layout**: time-series queries are almost always time-range scans with aggregations (`avg(cpu) over 5m windows grouped by host`). TSDBs partition by time (chunks), so a query touching the last hour scans only recent chunks, not the entire dataset. Pre-computed downsampling rollups (`5m avg`, `1h max`) mean historical queries read aggregated rollups, not raw points. The result: InfluxDB can return a 1-year chart in <100ms by reading the 1h rollup, while PostgreSQL would scan and aggregate millions of raw rows. These optimizations are workload-specific — they don't help with ad-hoc queries, joins, or transactions, which is why TSDBs are specialized.
**Visual:**
```
Why TSDBs dominate time-series workloads:

[1] Storage engine:
    TSDB:    LSM-tree (append-only MemTable -> SSTable, sequential I/O)
             -> ~1M writes/sec per node
    PG/MySQL: B-tree (random read-modify-write, page splits)
             -> ~10k inserts/sec per node

[2] Compression (10-100x):
    timestamps:    delta-of-delta (regular sampling -> ~1 bit/ts vs 64)
    floats:        Gorilla XOR (slow-changing -> 10x compression)
    strings:       dictionary encoding (tag values -> int IDs)

[3] Query optimization:
    time-based chunking: query last 1h -> scan only recent chunks
    downsampling rollups: 1y chart reads 1h rollup, not millions of raw pts
    columnar scan: only read columns referenced in query

Combined: 10-100x throughput + 10-100x compression + sub-100ms queries
Trade-off: optimized for time-range scans, weak for joins/transactions
```

### Q2. Explain delta-of-delta timestamp encoding and Gorilla float encoding.
**Answer:** **Delta-of-delta timestamp encoding** (from Facebook's 2015 Gorilla paper) exploits the regularity of time-series sampling. For data sampled every 10 seconds, consecutive timestamps differ by 10. The *delta* (10) is constant, so the *delta-of-delta* (delta[i+1] - delta[i]) is 0. Encoding stores: if delta-of-delta is 0, write a single `0` bit; if it's small (within ±63), write `10` + 7 bits; if it's larger, write `110` or `111` + more bits. For regular sampling, almost all timestamps compress to 1 bit (vs. 64 bits uncompressed). Even irregular sampling (jitter ±1s) compresses to ~7 bits. **Gorilla XOR float encoding** exploits the slow change of real-world metrics (CPU, memory, latency). Consecutive float values are XOR'd bitwise; if XOR is 0 (no change), store a single `0` bit. If XOR is non-zero, store `1` + a compact encoding of the significant bits (leading zeros count, trailing zeros count, meaningful bits). For metrics that change slowly (CPU bouncing 0.42 → 0.43 → 0.41), the XOR has few significant bits, compressing to ~16 bits vs. 64 bits uncompressed. Real-world metrics achieve ~10× float compression. Both encodings are lossless (no precision lost). Combined with dictionary encoding for tag values, a TSDB achieves 10–100× compression over the raw data — meaning 1TB of raw metrics becomes 10–100GB on disk, fitting in RAM for fast queries. These encodings are used in InfluxDB, Prometheus, M3, and Atlas.
**Visual:**
```
Delta-of-delta timestamp encoding (regular 10s sampling):

  raw ts:        1700000000, 1700000010, 1700000020, 1700000030
  delta:                    10,          10,          10
  delta-of-delta:                        0,           0
  encoded bits:                1 bit       1 bit       1 bit
                             (vs 64 bits per ts uncompressed)

  Gorilla XOR float encoding (slow-changing CPU metric):
  raw:           0.4200, 0.4300, 0.4100, 0.4250
  XOR bits:           ?      small     small     small
  encoded:       ~16 bits each (vs 64 bits uncompressed)

  Combined compression: 10-100x typical
  -> 1TB raw metrics -> 10-100GB on disk (fits in RAM)
  -> lossless (no precision lost)

  Used in: InfluxDB, Prometheus, M3, Atlas, TimescaleDB compression
  Source: Facebook Gorilla paper (2015)
```

### Q3. What is downsampling, and why is it critical for time series at scale?
**Answer:** **Downsampling** (also called rollups or aggregation) is the pre-computation of aggregates (avg, max, min, sum, p99, count) over fixed time windows (1m, 5m, 1h, 1d) from raw data points. For example, from 60 1-second CPU samples, compute one 1-minute average. The rollup is stored alongside (or instead of) raw points. **Why it's critical**: (1) **Storage cost** — raw 1-second metrics for 1000 hosts over 1 year = 31.5 trillion points. At 100 bytes each, that's 3.15PB. Downsampling to 1-minute rollups (60× reduction) = 525B points / 52GB. Downsampling to 1-hour rollups (3600×) = 8.7B points / 870MB. Without downsampling, storage costs make long retention infeasible. (2) **Query speed** — a "1-year CPU trend" chart reading raw points would scan billions of rows; reading the 1-hour rollup scans ~8760 rows (one per hour), returning in milliseconds. (3) **Network transfer** — dashboards fetching 1M raw points to render a chart would saturate the network; fetching 1000 downsampled points is trivial. (4) **Retention policies** — typical pattern: raw 7 days (for debugging), 5m rollups 30 days (for recent dashboards), 1h rollups 1 year (for long-term trends), 1d rollups forever (for year-over-year comparison). Old raw data is expired or archived to S3. **Real-world**: Prometheus has built-in `recorded rules` for downsampling; InfluxDB has Continuous Queries; TimescaleDB has Continuous Aggregates; Netflix Atlas has automated rollup pipelines. The trade-off: downsampling loses precision (you can't recover the original 1s samples from a 1m average), so high-resolution data must be retained for as long as needed for forensic debugging.
**Visual:**
```
Downsampling: pre-compute aggregates over fixed windows

  Raw 1s CPU samples: 0.41, 0.42, 0.43, 0.44, 0.45, 0.40, ... (60 points)
                       \_________________ ____________________/
                                         V
  1m rollup:           avg=0.425, max=0.45, min=0.40, count=60   (1 point)

Storage impact (1000 hosts, 1 year):
  Raw 1s:        31.5T points  -> 3.15 PB (infeasible)
  1m rollup:     525B points   -> 52 GB
  1h rollup:     8.7B points   -> 870 MB
  1d rollup:     365k points   -> 36 KB

Typical retention policy:
  raw 1s:        7 days   (for debugging, high resolution)
  5m rollup:     30 days   (recent dashboards)
  1h rollup:     1 year    (long-term trends)
  1d rollup:     forever   (year-over-year)

Trade-off: downsampling loses precision
  -> retain high-resolution raw for as long as needed for forensics
```

### Q4. Compare InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, Prometheus, and QuestDB. When do you choose each?
**Answer:** **InfluxDB** (InfluxData, Go-based, purpose-built TSDB) — high write throughput (1M+ points/sec/node), built-in downsampling (Continuous Queries), Flux query language (functional), Telegraf agent ecosystem, Flux-based Kapacitor alerting. Choose when: pure time-series workload, want turnkey TSDB with rich ecosystem, don't need SQL or joins. **TimescaleDB** (PostgreSQL extension) — adds hypertables (automatic time-based partitioning) to PostgreSQL, retaining full SQL/JOIN/JSON/transaction support. Compression (delta-of-delta + Gorilla) approaches InfluxDB. Choose when: team knows PostgreSQL, need to JOIN time-series with relational data (e.g., sensor readings + sensor metadata), want ACID transactions, or want one database for both time-series and operational data. **Prometheus** (CNCF, the Kubernetes observability standard) — pull-based scraping model, PromQL query language, label-based dimensional model, built-in service discovery for K8s. Designed for metrics/alerting, not long-term storage (default 15-day retention). Choose when: Kubernetes monitoring, alerting (Alertmanager), want the CNCF ecosystem (Grafana integration is seamless). For long-term storage, pair with Thanos/Cortex/M3. **QuestDB** — column-oriented, SQL syntax, claims very high ingest throughput (millions of rows/sec), open-source. Choose when: SQL familiarity matters, want maximum ingest throughput, financial market data (latency-sensitive). **Amazon Timestream** — managed AWS, automatic tiering (memory → SSD → S3), SQL query. Choose when: AWS shop, want zero ops. The choice depends on ecosystem fit: K8s observability → Prometheus; PG team + mixed workload → TimescaleDB; pure TSDB → InfluxDB; SQL + max throughput → QuestDB; managed AWS → Timestream.
**Visual:**
```
              InfluxDB     TimescaleDB    Prometheus    QuestDB      Timestream
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Engine        purpose-built PostgreSQL ext purpose-built columnar      managed AWS
Query lang    InfluxQL/Flux SQL            PromQL        SQL          SQL
Joins         weak          YES (full SQL) weak          YES          YES
ACID          no            YES            no            no           no
Ecosystem     Telegraf      PG ecosystem   K8s/CNCF      SQL          AWS
Long-term     YES (CQ)      YES            NO (15d def)  YES          YES (auto-tier)
Best for      pure TS       mixed workload K8s monitor   max ingest   managed AWS

Decision:
  + Kubernetes observability + alerting      -> Prometheus (+ Thanos for long-term)
  + PostgreSQL team + mixed workload          -> TimescaleDB
  + pure TS workload + rich TSDB ecosystem    -> InfluxDB
  + SQL + maximum ingest throughput           -> QuestDB
  + AWS shop, zero ops                        -> Amazon Timestream
  + IoT telemetry at massive scale            -> InfluxDB or TimescaleDB
```

### Q5. Why do TSDBs struggle with high-cardinality labels, and how do you mitigate it?
**Answer:** High-cardinality labels (e.g., `user_id`, `request_id`, `session_id` as a label) cause **series explosion**. In Prometheus/InfluxDB, each unique combination of metric name + label values = one time series. If you have `http_requests_total{user_id="..."}` with 1M users, you have 1M series — each with its own in-memory index entry, chunk metadata, and ingestion path. Prometheus scales to ~10M series per server; beyond that, memory blows up, query planning slows, and ingestion lags. The root cause: TSDBs are optimized for *low-cardinality labels* (host, region, env, service — typically dozens to thousands of values), where the series count is bounded. High-cardinality labels violate this assumption. **Mitigations**: (1) **Don't use high-cardinality values as labels** — keep user_id, request_id, session_id in logs (Elasticsearch/Loki), not in metrics. Metrics are for aggregates (`http_requests_total{status="200", endpoint="/api/users"}`); logs are for individual events. (2) **Pre-aggregate at write time** — instead of `http_requests_total{user_id="42"}`, emit `http_requests_total{endpoint="/api/users", status="200"}` and lose the user_id dimension. (3) **Use histograms** — for latency, use `http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.1"}` (a few dozen buckets) instead of one series per request. (4) **Use a high-cardinality-capable TSDB** — TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL-indexed, handles billions of rows), Druid (designed for high-cardinality analytics), or ClickHouse (columnar with dictionary encoding, handles cardinality well). (5) **Partition by tenant** — for multi-tenant SaaS, one TSDB instance per tenant (or per N tenants), bounding per-instance cardinality. **Real-world**: Discord migrated from Prometheus to a custom high-cardinality TSDB because per-user and per-server metrics blew up Prometheus's memory.
**Visual:**
```
Series explosion from high-cardinality labels:

  Low cardinality (good):
    http_requests_total{host="web-1", status="200"}   -> 1 series
    http_requests_total{host="web-1", status="500"}   -> 1 series
    Total: ~1000 series (100 hosts x 10 status codes)

  High cardinality (BAD):
    http_requests_total{user_id="42", endpoint="/api"}   -> 1 series per user!
    Total: 1M series (1M users) -> Prometheus memory blows up

Mitigations:
  [1] Don't use high-cardinality values as labels
      user_id, request_id, session_id -> LOGS (Elasticsearch/Loki), not metrics
  [2] Pre-aggregate at write time
      emit http_requests_total{endpoint, status} (lose user_id dimension)
  [3] Use histograms (latency buckets, not per-request series)
      http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.1"}
  [4] Use high-cardinality-capable TSDB
      TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL-indexed), Druid, ClickHouse
  [5] Partition by tenant (one TSDB per N tenants)

Rule: metrics = aggregates; logs = individual events.
      High-cardinality dimensions belong in logs, not metrics.
```

### Q6. How do retention policies work, and what's the typical multi-tier strategy?
**Answer:** A **retention policy** specifies how long data is kept at each resolution. Time-series data has a natural lifecycle: recent data is queried frequently (for dashboards and alerting) and needs high resolution; old data is queried rarely (for trend analysis) and can be downsampled. The typical multi-tier strategy: **Tier 1 (hot, recent)** — raw high-resolution data (1s or 10s samples), kept in RAM or fast SSD, retained for 7-30 days. Powers real-time dashboards and short-term alerting. **Tier 2 (warm)** — downsampled to 1m or 5m rollups, kept on SSD, retained for 30-90 days. Powers recent historical dashboards and weekly reports. **Tier 3 (cold)** — downsampled to 1h rollups, kept on HDD or object storage (S3), retained for 1-5 years. Powers long-term trend analysis and capacity planning. **Tier 4 (archive)** — downsampled to 1d rollups, kept on S3/Glacier, retained indefinitely. Powers year-over-year comparison and compliance. **Mechanics**: (1) In InfluxDB, retention policies (RP) define duration; Continuous Queries (CQ) automatically downsample from one RP to another. (2) In TimescaleDB, `drop_after` policies and Continuous Aggregates handle this. (3) In Prometheus, retention is configured globally (`--storage.tsdb.retention.time=15d`); for multi-tier, use Thanos (long-term storage on S3 with downsampling). (4) In Amazon Timestream, tiering is automatic (memory → SSD → S3 with configurable transition times). **Cost**: a 1000-host deployment at 1s resolution would generate ~31B points/year — at 100 bytes each, 3.1PB. With multi-tier retention, total storage drops to <100GB (rollups dominate), making long retention economically feasible.
**Visual:**
```
Multi-tier retention strategy:

  Tier     Resolution   Storage     Retention   Use case
  -----    ----------   --------    ----------  -----------------------
  Hot      raw 1s       RAM/SSD     7-30 days   real-time dashboards, alerting
  Warm     1m rollup    SSD         30-90 days  recent history, weekly reports
  Cold     1h rollup    HDD/S3      1-5 years   long-term trends, capacity planning
  Archive  1d rollup    S3/Glacier  indefinite  year-over-year, compliance

  Mechanisms:
    InfluxDB:     Retention Policies (RP) + Continuous Queries (CQ)
    TimescaleDB:  drop_after policy + Continuous Aggregates
    Prometheus:   --storage.tsdb.retention.time=15d + Thanos for S3
    Timestream:   automatic tiering (memory -> SSD -> S3)

  Cost example (1000 hosts, 1 year):
    Raw 1s:        31B points -> 3.1 PB (infeasible)
    Hot 7d raw:    600M points -> 60 GB SSD
    Warm 90d 1m:   130M points -> 13 GB SSD
    Cold 5y 1h:    44M points -> 4.4 GB HDD
    Archive 1d:    365k points -> 36 KB S3
    Total: <100 GB (vs 3.1 PB without downsampling)
```

### Q7. How does Prometheus's pull model differ from InfluxDB's push model, and what are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** **Prometheus** uses a **pull model** — the Prometheus server actively scrapes metrics endpoints (`/metrics`) on a configured interval (default 15s). Service discovery (Kubernetes API, Consul, EC2) tells Prometheus which targets to scrape. Each scrape is an HTTP GET that returns metrics in text format. **InfluxDB** uses a **push model** — applications and agents (Telegraf) push metrics to InfluxDB via HTTP/UDP, batching writes for efficiency. **Trade-offs of pull (Prometheus)**: (1) **Centralized control** — the server decides what to scrape and how often; no agent misconfiguration can flood the server. (2) **Health check built-in** — if a scrape fails, Prometheus records the target as down (an "up" metric), giving you free availability monitoring. (3) **Easy debugging** — `curl http://service:9090/metrics` shows exactly what the server sees. (4) **No agent to deploy** — applications expose an HTTP endpoint; no separate agent process. (5) **Drawback: doesn't cross firewalls easily** — pull requires the server to reach the target; for ephemeral or behind-NAT targets (laptops, IoT behind carrier NAT), push is necessary. (6) **Drawback: short-lived jobs** — a cron job that runs for 5s may be missed by a 15s scrape; Prometheus has a PushGateway for this (anti-pattern for general use). **Trade-offs of push (InfluxDB)**: (1) **Crosses firewalls** — agents initiate outbound connections, friendly to NAT/firewalls. (2) **Batching efficiency** — agents batch many metrics per request, amortizing network overhead. (3) **Drawback: agent management** — must deploy and configure Telegraf on every host. (4) **Drawback: no implicit health check** — if an agent crashes, no metric is pushed; you need separate heartbeat monitoring. (5) **Drawback: rogue agents can flood** — a misconfigured agent can swamp the server. **Real-world**: K8s/cloud-native → Prometheus pull; IoT/edge/legacy → InfluxDB push; mixed environments → both, with Telegraf scraping Prometheus exposition format.
**Visual:**
```
Pull model (Prometheus):
  Prometheus server -> scrape /metrics every 15s -> service A, B, C
  Service discovery (K8s API, Consul, EC2) -> tells server what to scrape

  Pros:
    + centralized control (server decides what/when)
    + free health check ("up" metric = scrape succeeded)
    + easy debugging (curl /metrics)
    + no agent to deploy
  Cons:
    - doesn't cross firewalls/NAT
    - short-lived jobs missed (PushGateway is anti-pattern for general use)

Push model (InfluxDB):
  Telegraf agent -> batch metrics -> HTTP/UDP -> InfluxDB
  Application -> InfluxDB client library -> direct push

  Pros:
    + crosses firewalls/NAT (outbound)
    + batching efficiency (agent batches, amortizes network)
  Cons:
    - agent to deploy and configure (Telegraf on every host)
    - no implicit health check (agent crash = no metric)
    - rogue agents can flood server

When:
  + K8s/cloud-native           -> Prometheus pull
  + IoT/edge/behind NAT        -> InfluxDB push
  + Mixed env                  -> both (Telegraf can scrape Prom exposition)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Netflix wants to monitor 10,000 microservices with CPU, memory, request latency, and error-rate metrics at 10-second resolution, retaining 1 year for trend analysis. How do you architect this?
**Answer:** Architecture: **(1) Collection** — each microservice exposes a `/metrics` endpoint in Prometheus exposition format; a Prometheus server (or Cortex/M3 for federation) scrapes every 10s. Service discovery via Kubernetes API auto-discovers pods. **(2) Storage** — at 10k services × ~100 metrics each × 6 samples/min = 6M points/min = 100k points/sec. A single Prometheus handles ~1M points/sec, but for HA and scale, use **Thanos** (or Cortex, or M3) for federation + long-term storage on S3. Each Prometheus handles a subset (e.g., 1 per cluster, ~1000 services). **(3) Multi-tier retention**: hot raw 10s data for 7 days (for debugging), 1m rollups for 30 days (recent dashboards), 1h rollups for 1 year (trends). Thanos Compactor automatically downsamples raw to 5m and 1h rollups and stores on S3. **(4) Query layer** — Grafana for dashboards, querying Thanos Querier which federates across all Prometheus instances + S3. **(5) Alerting** — Alertmanager routes alerts (e.g., `error_rate > 1% for 2m` → page on-call; `p99 latency > 500ms for 5m` → Slack). **(6) Cardinality discipline** — labels are limited to low-cardinality dimensions (service, env, region, method, status); user_id and request_id stay in logs (Elasticsearch), not metrics. **(7) Capacity**: 10k services × 100 metrics × 10s = 100k points/sec; 1 year at 10s = 315B points raw = ~30TB compressed (10× compression); with downsampling to 1h rollups, 1-year storage is <100GB. **(8) Anomaly detection** — Netflix's Atlas anomaly detection flags unusual patterns (sudden latency spike, error burst) automatically. This is essentially Netflix's actual architecture (Atlas + Elasticsearch + Grafana).
**Visual:**
```
Netflix metrics architecture (10k microservices, 1y retention):

  Microservices (10k) -> /metrics endpoint (Prom exposition format)
       |
       | scrape every 10s
       v
  Prometheus servers (10-20, sharded by cluster, ~1k services each)
       |
       +--- local storage (15d raw, fast SSD)
       |
       +--- Thanos Sidecar -> upload blocks to S3
                                |
                                v
                          Thanos Store Gateway
                                |
       Thanos Querier <--------+
       (federates across Prom + S3)
       |
       +--- Grafana dashboards (real-time + historical)
       +--- Alertmanager (page on-call if error > 1% / p99 > 500ms)
       +--- Atlas anomaly detection (unusual pattern alerts)

  Multi-tier retention:
    Hot raw 10s:  7 days   (SSD, for debugging)
    5m rollup:    30 days  (SSD, recent dashboards)
    1h rollup:    1 year   (S3 via Thanos Compactor, trends)

  Cardinality discipline:
    labels = service, env, region, method, status (low-cardinality)
    user_id, request_id -> logs (Elasticsearch), NOT metrics

  Capacity:
    100k pts/sec ingest (10k svc x 100 metrics x 0.1/sec)
    1y raw: ~30TB compressed -> downsampled to <100GB rollups
```

### Q2. Uber's M3 needs to handle 500M metrics/sec across 50,000 hosts. How does M3 achieve this scale?
**Answer:** Uber built M3 (open-sourced, Prometheus-compatible) to handle scale that vanilla Prometheus couldn't. Architecture: **(1) M3 Coordinator** — sidecar on every host, accepts metrics from local applications and the local Prometheus, batches and forwards to M3DB. **(2) M3DB** — the distributed TSDB, sharded by metric name + labels hash across hundreds of nodes. Uses dynamic cluster sharding (consistent hashing) for rebalancing. Storage engine: LSM-tree with columnar compression (delta-of-delta + Gorilla) — ~50× compression. **(3) Replication** — RF=3 across racks/DCs for durability; quorum writes for consistency. **(4) Downsampling** — automated pipeline that downsamples raw 10s data to 1m and 1h rollups in the background. **(5) Retention** — configurable per metric namespace (e.g., infrastructure metrics 30 days raw + 1y rollups; business metrics 7d raw + 90d rollups). **(6) Query layer** — M3 Query federates across M3DB shards, supports PromQL + Graphite + custom query language. **(7) Scale**: 500M metrics/sec × 100 bytes = 50GB/sec ingest; compressed ~1GB/sec; 1 year = ~30PB raw / ~600TB compressed across the cluster. **(8) Multi-DC** — M3DB clusters in each region with cross-region replication for disaster recovery. **(9) Cardinality management** — M3 is designed for higher cardinality than Prometheus (custom indexing), but still warns against user_id-level labels. **(10) Operational tooling** — M3 Aggregator for downsampling, M3 Coordinator for ingestion, M3DB for storage, M3 Query for queries — all integrated. Uber migrated from Prometheus + Thanos to M3 because Thanos's S3-based architecture couldn't keep up with their ingest rate.
**Visual:**
```
Uber M3 architecture (500M metrics/sec, 50k hosts):

  Hosts (50k) -> M3 Coordinator (sidecar)
                   |
                   | batch + forward
                   v
                M3DB cluster (hundreds of nodes, consistent hashing)
                   |
                   +--- RF=3 across racks/DCs (quorum writes)
                   +--- LSM-tree + columnar compression (50x)
                   +--- automated downsampling (10s -> 1m -> 1h)
                   +--- retention per namespace (30d raw + 1y rollup)
                   |
                   v
                M3 Query (federates across shards)
                   |
                   +--- Grafana dashboards
                   +--- Alertmanager
                   +--- autoscaling triggers

  Scale:
    500M metrics/sec x 100 bytes = 50 GB/sec ingest
    compressed: ~1 GB/sec
    1 year: ~30 PB raw / ~600 TB compressed across cluster

  Multi-DC: M3DB in each region, cross-region replication for DR

  Why M3 over Prometheus + Thanos:
    + higher cardinality tolerance (custom indexing)
    + native distributed storage (no S3 dependency for ingest path)
    + integrated downsampling (M3 Aggregator)
    + Uber's ingest rate exceeded Thanos's S3-based architecture

  Open-sourced (CNCF-compatible), Prometheus query compatible
```

### Q3. Tesla wants to ingest telemetry (battery, motor, GPS) from 5M vehicles at 1Hz. How do you architect this?
**Answer:** Scale: 5M vehicles × ~20 metrics × 1 sample/sec = 100M points/sec ingest. Architecture: **(1) Vehicle-side aggregation** — vehicles batch locally (10-60s of data) and upload via cellular/Wi-Fi every minute, not real-time. This reduces ingest rate to ~5M points/sec (10× reduction) and tolerates connectivity gaps. **(2) Ingest layer** — Kafka as the ingestion buffer (handles bursts when vehicles reconnect after offline periods); Kafka partitioned by `vehicle_id` for per-vehicle ordering. **(3) Storage** — TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL extension) or InfluxDB clustered. TimescaleDB chosen if you need to JOIN telemetry with vehicle metadata (model, firmware version, owner). At 5M points/sec × 100 bytes = 500MB/sec = ~43TB/day compressed ~4-5TB/day; 1-year retention = ~1.6PB. **(4) Partitioning** — by `vehicle_id` hash + time chunk (1h); each vehicle's telemetry stays in one shard for fast per-vehicle queries. **(5) Downsampling** — 1Hz raw for 7 days (forensic debugging), 1-minute rollups for 90 days (recent dashboards), 1-hour rollups for 5 years (long-term trends, warranty analysis). **(6) Cardinality** — `vehicle_id` is high-cardinality (5M values), but TimescaleDB handles this well (PostgreSQL-indexed). Prometheus would die at this cardinality. **(7) Real-time alerting** — stream processing (Kafka Streams / Flink) flags anomalies (battery temperature > threshold, sudden motor fault) and triggers warranty/service workflows. **(8) Cold storage** — 1-year+ data archived to S3 (Glacier for 5+ year) for compliance and warranty disputes. **(9) Query patterns**: per-vehicle timeline (`SELECT * FROM telemetry WHERE vehicle_id=X AND time > ...`), fleet aggregates (`AVG(battery_temp) GROUP BY model, region`), anomaly queries. **(10) Privacy** — GPS data is PII; encrypt per-vehicle; aggregate for analytics. This is essentially what Tesla (and other connected-vehicle manufacturers) run.
**Visual:**
```
Tesla vehicle telemetry (5M vehicles, 1Hz):

  Vehicles (5M) -> local batch (10-60s) -> upload every minute via cellular
       |
       v
  Kafka (ingest buffer, partitioned by vehicle_id)
       |
       +--- Kafka Streams / Flink (real-time anomaly detection)
       |     -> battery temp > threshold -> trigger service alert
       |
       v
  TimescaleDB cluster (or InfluxDB clustered)
       |
       +--- partition by vehicle_id hash + 1h time chunk
       +--- compression: delta-of-delta + Gorilla (~10x)
       +--- downsampling: 1Hz raw 7d, 1m rollup 90d, 1h rollup 5y
       +--- 1y retention: ~1.6 PB compressed
       |
       +--- per-vehicle queries: SELECT * FROM telemetry WHERE vehicle_id=X
       +--- fleet aggregates: AVG(battery_temp) GROUP BY model, region
       |
       v
  Cold storage: 1y+ to S3/Glacier (warranty disputes, compliance)

  Why TimescaleDB over Prometheus:
    + vehicle_id is high-cardinality (5M values) -> Prometheus would die
    + need to JOIN telemetry with vehicle metadata (model, firmware)
    + PostgreSQL-indexed handles billions of rows

  Real-world: Tesla, Rivian, Ford, BMW connected-vehicle platforms
```

### Q4. A startup needs to choose between Prometheus and InfluxDB for monitoring a 50-service K8s cluster. How do you decide?
**Answer:** For a 50-service K8s cluster, **Prometheus is the default choice**. Reasoning: **(1) Ecosystem fit** — Prometheus is the CNCF standard for Kubernetes monitoring. Helm charts, the kube-prometheus-stack, and most K8s exporters (kube-state-metrics, node-exporter) are built for Prometheus. Service discovery via the K8s API auto-discovers pods; you don't configure targets manually. **(2) Operational simplicity** — Prometheus deploys as a single StatefulSet; default 15-day retention is fine for a startup. Grafana has a first-class Prometheus data source with ready-made dashboards (e.g., the "Kubernetes Cluster" dashboard). Alertmanager handles routing (email/Slack/PagerDuty). **(3) PromQL** — purpose-built for time-series operations (`rate()`, `histogram_quantile()`, `predict_linear()`). For monitoring queries, PromQL is more expressive than InfluxQL. **(4) Cost** — open-source, runs on a single node for 50 services (~$100/month EC2 instance). **(5) Pull model** — natural for K8s (server scrapes pods via service discovery). **Choose InfluxDB instead if**: (a) you need to ingest non-K8s metrics from IoT/edge devices behind NAT (push model needed); (b) you want long-term retention >15 days without adding Thanos (InfluxDB has native long-term storage); (c) you're already using Telegraf for log/metric collection and want a unified stack; (d) you need to JOIN time-series with relational data (InfluxDB Flux can do this, but TimescaleDB is better). **For 50 services, scale is not the deciding factor** — both handle it. The deciding factor is ecosystem: Prometheus is the K8s default; deviate only if you have a specific reason. Most startups run Prometheus + Grafana + Alertmanager and add Thanos/Cortex when they outgrow single-node Prometheus.
**Visual:**
```
50-service K8s cluster: Prometheus vs InfluxDB

  Default: PROMETHEUS
  Reasoning:
    [1] Ecosystem fit (CNCF standard, K8s exporters, Helm charts)
    [2] Operational simplicity (1 StatefulSet, default 15d retention)
    [3] PromQL purpose-built for monitoring queries
       (rate(), histogram_quantile(), predict_linear())
    [4] Cost (open-source, single node ~$100/mo EC2)
    [5] Pull model + K8s service discovery (auto-discovers pods)

  Choose INFLUXDB if:
    + ingest non-K8s metrics from IoT/edge behind NAT (push model)
    + want >15d retention without adding Thanos
    + already using Telegraf, want unified stack
    + need Flux query language (more flexible than PromQL for complex analytics)

  For 50 services, scale is NOT the deciding factor (both handle it).
  Deciding factor: ecosystem fit -> Prometheus is K8s default.

  Standard startup stack:
    Prometheus + Grafana + Alertmanager
    + add Thanos/Cortex when outgrowing single-node (typically 200+ services)
```

### Q5. You're seeing Prometheus memory blow up at 30GB with only 1000 hosts. How do you diagnose and fix it?
**Answer:** **Diagnosis**: Prometheus memory is dominated by the in-memory index of active time series. 30GB for 1000 hosts suggests series explosion — likely a high-cardinality label. **Step 1: Identify high-cardinality labels** — query Prometheus's `prometheus_tsdb_head_series` metric (active series count); if it's >10M, you have a problem. Use PromQL: `topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))` shows the metrics with the most series. Look for labels with thousands of unique values. **Step 2: Check for accidental high-cardinality labels** — common culprits: `user_id`, `request_id`, `session_id`, `trace_id`, `path` (with query strings), `instance` (with ephemeral pod IPs). Inspect a sample of the offending metric: `http_requests_total{user_id="42", user_id="43", ...}` = bad. **Step 3: Fix the source** — remove the high-cardinality label from the metric definition. Use logs (Loki, Elasticsearch) for per-user/request dimensions, not metrics. Re-deploy the service with the fixed metric. **Step 4: Reduce retention if needed** — `--storage.tsdb.retention.time=15d` (or even 7d) reduces active series. **Step 5: Increase memory or shard** — if legitimate (you really need that cardinality), add memory or run multiple Prometheus instances sharded by service/namespace (Thanos/Cortex federation). **Step 6: Use relabeling** — Prometheus's `relabel_configs` can drop high-cardinality labels at scrape time (`metric_relabel_configs` with `labeldrop`). **Step 7: Monitor going forward** — alert on `prometheus_tsdb_head_series > 5M` to catch cardinality growth early. **Real-world**: Discord migrated off Prometheus because per-user and per-server metrics blew up memory; they built a custom TSDB. Many companies hit this at ~10M series and either shard Prometheus or migrate to a high-cardinality-capable TSDB.
**Visual:**
```
Prometheus memory blow-up diagnosis:

  Symptom: 30GB RAM for 1000 hosts (should be <5GB)

  Step 1: Check active series count
    prometheus_tsdb_head_series -> if >10M, series explosion

  Step 2: Find high-cardinality labels
    topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))
    -> identify metric with most series
    -> inspect: http_requests_total{user_id="42", user_id="43", ...} = BAD

  Step 3: Common culprits
    user_id, request_id, session_id, trace_id, path (with query strings),
    instance (ephemeral pod IPs)

  Step 4: Fixes
    [a] Remove high-cardinality label from metric definition
        (use logs for per-user/request dimensions, not metrics)
    [b] Reduce retention: --storage.tsdb.retention.time=7d
    [c] Drop labels at scrape time:
        metric_relabel_configs:
          - action: labeldrop
            regex: "user_id|request_id"
    [d] Shard Prometheus (one per namespace/service)
        + Thanos/Cortex federation
    [e] Migrate to high-cardinality TSDB (TimescaleDB, ClickHouse, Druid)

  Step 5: Monitor going forward
    alert on prometheus_tsdb_head_series > 5M

  Real-world: Discord migrated off Prometheus for this reason
```

### Q6. An IoT company has 1M devices each sending a temperature reading every 10 seconds. Storage is expensive. How do you design for cost efficiency?
**Answer:** Scale: 1M devices × 0.1 samples/sec = 100k points/sec = 8.6B points/day. At 100 bytes each, ~860GB/day uncompressed. **Cost-efficient design**: **(1) Compression** — choose a TSDB with strong compression (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB). Delta-of-delta timestamps (regular 10s sampling → ~1 bit/ts) + Gorilla floats (slow-changing temperature → ~16 bits/value) + dictionary strings (device_id → int ID) achieve ~30-50× compression. 860GB → ~20GB/day. **(2) Aggressive downsampling** — IoT temperature data rarely needs 10s resolution beyond a day. Retention policy: raw 10s for 7 days (~140GB), 1m rollups for 30 days (~6GB), 1h rollups for 1 year (~700MB), 1d rollups forever (~10MB). Total hot storage: ~150GB. **(3) Edge aggregation** — devices batch locally (60-600s of readings) and upload every minute, reducing ingest rate 6-60× and tolerating connectivity gaps. **(4) Cold storage** — data older than 1 year goes to S3 Glacier ($0.004/GB-month vs. SSD $0.10/GB-month). 1-year of 1d rollups = ~10MB, essentially free. **(5) Multi-tier storage** — InfluxDB Enterprise has tiered storage (RAM/SSD/HDD/S3); Amazon Timestream auto-tiers; TimescaleDB can partition old chunks to cheaper table spaces. **(6) Cardinality control** — `device_id` is high-cardinality (1M values); use TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL-indexed, handles this) or InfluxDB (also handles 1M series). Avoid Prometheus. **(7) Lossy compression for old data** — for 1y+ data, consider lossy downsampling (e.g., keep only daily min/max/avg, dropping hourly). **(8) Data lifecycle automation** — InfluxDB Continuous Queries auto-downsample; TimescaleDB Continuous Aggregates; cron jobs for S3 archival. **Total annual cost**: ~150GB hot SSD ($15/month) + ~5GB cold S3 ($0.02/month) = under $20/month storage, vs. ~$860/month for raw uncompressed retention. Real-world: Tesla, Nest, and industrial IoT providers use these patterns.
**Visual:**
```
IoT temperature at 1M devices x 1 sample/10s = 100k pts/sec = 8.6B/day

  Cost-efficient design:
  [1] Compression (30-50x)
      delta-of-delta ts (10s regular -> ~1 bit)
      Gorilla floats (slow temperature -> ~16 bits)
      dictionary strings (device_id -> int ID)
      -> 860 GB/day uncompressed -> ~20 GB/day compressed
  [2] Aggressive downsampling
      raw 10s:        7 days   (~140 GB SSD)
      1m rollup:      30 days  (~6 GB SSD)
      1h rollup:      1 year   (~700 MB HDD)
      1d rollup:      forever  (~10 MB S3)
      Total hot: ~150 GB
  [3] Edge aggregation (devices batch 60-600s, upload every minute)
      -> 6-60x ingest reduction + tolerates gaps
  [4] Cold storage (S3 Glacier, $0.004/GB-mo vs SSD $0.10/GB-mo)
  [5] Multi-tier storage (RAM -> SSD -> HDD -> S3)
  [6] Cardinality control (1M device_id -> TimescaleDB or InfluxDB, NOT Prometheus)
  [7] Lossy for old data (1y+ keeps daily min/max/avg only)
  [8] Automated lifecycle (InfluxDB CQ, TimescaleDB CAGG, cron for S3)

  Cost: ~$20/month storage (vs ~$860/month raw uncompressed)
  Real-world: Tesla, Nest, industrial IoT providers
```

### Q7. You need real-time alerting on a 5-second window: "if error rate > 1% for 5s, page on-call." How do you architect this with a TSDB?
**Answer:** 5-second alerting is at the edge of what most TSDBs handle natively (Prometheus default scrape is 15s; InfluxDB is push-based so faster). Architecture: **(1) High-resolution ingestion** — applications push metrics every 1-2s (or stream events to Kafka and aggregate in stream). For 5s windows, you need at least 1s resolution. **(2) Stream processing for sub-TSDB latency** — for true 5s alerting, don't rely on the TSDB; use a stream processor (Kafka Streams, Flink, Esper) that maintains a rolling 5s window in memory and emits alerts directly. The TSDB still stores the metrics for dashboards and historical analysis. **(3) Prometheus with 5s scrape** — if you use Prometheus, configure `scrape_interval: 5s` (increases load 3×). Alert rule: `ALERT HighErrorRate IF rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5s]) / rate(http_requests_total[5s]) > 0.01 FOR 5s`. Alertmanager routes to PagerDuty. **(4) Recording rules** — pre-compute the error rate every 5s into a recorded metric (`error_rate_5s`) so the alert rule is fast. **(5) Avoid alert flapping** — `FOR 5s` means the condition must persist for 5s (one full window) before alerting; without it, a single 5s blip would page. **(6) Use histograms** — for latency alerts, use `histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5s])) > 0.5` — pre-bucketed, fast to compute. **(7) Push-based for fastest** — if you need <1s alerting, push events directly to a stream processor (Flink) that maintains tumbling windows and emits alerts; the TSDB is downstream for dashboards. **(8) Alerting best practices**: page on SLO burn rate (multi-window: 2% budget in 1h = page; 5% in 6h = ticket), not raw thresholds, to avoid noise. **Real-world**: Netflix uses Atlas for sub-minute alerting; Uber uses M3 with custom alerting; Google's SRE book recommends multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting.
**Visual:**
```
5-second alerting architecture:

  Option A: TSDB-based (5s scrape interval)
    App -> /metrics (every 5s) -> Prometheus (scrape_interval: 5s)
    -> recording rule: error_rate_5s = rate(http_requests_total{status=5xx}[5s])
                                   / rate(http_requests_total[5s])
    -> alert rule:
         ALERT HighErrorRate
         IF error_rate_5s > 0.01
         FOR 5s   (condition persists for full window -> avoid flapping)
    -> Alertmanager -> PagerDuty

  Option B: Stream-based (for <5s alerting)
    App -> events -> Kafka -> Flink/Kafka Streams
      -> maintain rolling 5s window in memory
      -> if error_rate > 0.01, emit alert directly to Alertmanager
      -> TSDB stores metrics for dashboards (downstream)

  Best practices:
    + recording rules (pre-compute error_rate_5s, don't recompute on alert)
    + FOR 5s clause (avoid flapping on single blip)
    + histograms for latency (pre-bucketed, fast quantile computation)
    + SLO burn-rate alerting (multi-window: 2% budget/1h -> page;
                              5% budget/6h -> ticket) -> avoid noise

  Trade-off:
    Prometheus scrape_interval: 5s (3x load vs default 15s)
    For <1s alerting: must use stream processor (TSDB adds latency)

  Real-world:
    Netflix Atlas (sub-minute alerting)
    Uber M3 (custom alerting)
    Google SRE book: multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting
```
